description_full: Keller Group plc provides specialist geotechnical services in North America, Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific. The company offers ground engineering solutions, including ground improvement services, grouting, deep foundations, earth retention, marine, and instrumentation and monitoring services, as well as post-tension systems and industrial services. It also provides bearing capacity/ settlement control, low carbon construction, containment, excavation support, stabilization, marine structures, seepage control, slope stabilization, and monitoring solutions. In addition, it provides environmental remediation and demolition. The company provides its services to the construction sector in commercial, industrial, infrastructure, institutional/public buildings, power, and residential markets. Keller Group plc was founded in 1860 and is headquartered in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: KELLER GROUP PLC is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.7B market cap on $4.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 8% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 70% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $224M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.81× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.3×.
Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.1% of the shares.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 115% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 10% over the last three months.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 0.58, it is more defensive than the market.

val: The stock trades 55% below its DCF fair value of $91.19, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $69.26 to $125 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 13.9 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 9.6 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 12.2 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 8.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 7.9% annual cash-flow growth, 17pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 7.5% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It runs a 70% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.81x.
ROE of 22% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.9x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($370.6M of cash against $414.6M of debt), with interest covered 8.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.8% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 18% of profits supports about 3.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 5.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 2.6% in dividends).
people: With about 10,000 employees, each generates about $412K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median.
That works out to $22K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
